payload.do: Report verified facts; mark unsupported claims `UNKNOWN`.
Always ask yourself: 'Do we really need this? Can we do it simpler and more reliably?' Keep the solution extensible, minimal, and reliable. Do not overengineer.
Use English. Russian allowed with Owner.

payload.rule: Separate lane checks from operator checks after landing. Lane checks must run in the container. Preserve every AC and required pre-landing gate. Operator checks cannot replace verification-only acceptance checks. Review every AC against evidence. In lane Tasks, live acceptance bindings, report publication and deployment are operator checks. Keep operator checks pending at to_test until evidence exists. Never report pending checks as passed. Compare only the failing relevant check with the base when diagnosis needs it. Do not require routine base-commit check runs or an unrelated baseline suite.

A code Task owns one production module, its required migrations, and tests for approved behavior, regardless of directory layout. Keep help text that ships inside the module with its Task. Other production modules need separate Tasks. Create documentation Tasks only when the AC explicitly requires a document. Read current Tasks under the same Requirement or related NTK tickets before creating work. Check other related work when reuse crosses Requirements. Reuse the Task that owns a shared mechanism. Add dependencies on required outputs. Plan only missing behavior. Never assign the same change to multiple Tasks. Never weaken checks or expand approved behavior. For execution, modulePaths defines the writable roots when supplied.
Prefix shell commands with `rtk`. Use `rtk proxy <command>` when unfiltered output is needed.

Write new prose in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (Issue 9). At least 80% of sentences in each text must comply. Apply this standard to all new prose that you write, including reports, reviews, signal messages, code comments, commit messages and ticket text. Limit instructions to 20 words and descriptions to 25 words. Use one action per instruction, active voice, simple tenses, imperative instructions, common words, and consistent terms. Limit noun groups to three words. Avoid contractions, omitted words, and semicolons. Limit each paragraph to one topic and six sentences. Use vertical lists for complex text. Start warnings with a command or condition. Then state the risk. Preserve code, commands, identifiers, quotes, logs, existing records and required output formats.
